speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though my hon. friend notified me that he intended to ask this question, I *can only tell him that there have been no important new developments to justify me in making anything like an optimistic statement in the house today.

I wonder whether the minister will explain why his department's record regarding the expenditure of money voted last year is so much better for Nova Scotia than for the other provinces. We pointed out, for instance, yesterday that eight of the nine items listed for Newfoundland were revotes, that seven of these were entirely revotes for projects on which nothing had been done during the year. In the case of Nova Scotia there are only nine out of fourteen revotes and only four of these are entire revotes. In other words, out of fourteen projects ten were started. A year ago the department estimated they had asked for $360,000 more than they were able to spend, yet they actually asked for $780,000 more than they did expend, which is only about twice as much as they estimated. In the case of Newfoundland they left unspent about four times as much as they estimated would be unspent. There may be some circumstances which explain why the department is so much more efficient in spending the moneys voted for Nova Scotia than for Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT

There is just one
explanation I can give the hon. member. Newfoundland joined Canada only four years ago, and we had to set up in that province a district. We had to have people from headquarters go out to Newfoundland and make a study of the situation. Probably the progress is not as rapid there as it would be in a province which joined confederation in 1867, where we have an old staff and know the situation. That would be one reason.

The second reason probably is that our staff in Newfoundland is not extensive enough, and we were most ambitious in our estimates of the work we could do. The hon. gentleman who hails from that province would know that every Canadian wants to keep the friendship of that new province, and my department especially is doing its utmost to meet their requests and try to do the work they need done, but I think it will take me some time to succeed.

Less: Estimated amount by which actual expenditure on all listed projects will fall short of the total of amounts that may be required for each, $450,000. 

That leaves a total of $1,215,000. We know that in every instance we will not expend the whole amount, but I remember one year we spent $2 million more on a project than what we had asked for. Next year the probability is that more work will be done in the other province. The staff here in Ottawa cannot give the same attention to all parts of the country. When they start on certain projects they try to complete them.
I am not bragging when I say that I have had some experience in these matters as I have been handling this department for some time. Perhaps I should have a smile oh my face, but I know the matter is more serious. I am anxious to see buildings completed so that the country may have all the facilities required. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT

There are two or three questions I should like to bring up on this vote. The first has to do with the policy of the department in regard to putting up buildings and purchasing property in centres where there is a town plan. For example, in Vancouver we have a town plan and a town planning commission. The type of building that can be put in certain areas is governed by that plan.
There has been considerable trouble with the minister's department because of the fact that on some occasions the department has erected buildings in an area where office buildings are not supposed to go. We believe the department should do its utmost to cooperate in that regard. I hope the minister will adopt the policy of not breaking down the town plan in these centres and will put his buildings in a part of the city where private individuals can construct buildings of the same type. It is very unfair for the department to go into a one-family dwelling district and put up an office building. I see no reason for the department following a practice of that kind. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: I would not hesitate to give that assurance, because I want to keep our public relations at a high level, and would not want to lose the confidence of the people. I am told by the officials of the department that they try to conform to the planning in different towns and cities. In Vancouver we have three architects, and I would hope they would not advise us to erect buildings that would be contrary to any of the planning regulations of the city. However, I will give the assurance that the officials will co-operate with local authorities before putting up buildings.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext:
A further question of policy has to do with the refusal of the department to instal washroom facilities for the general public in public buildings. I realize that is a wise policy in respect of most buildings. However, in Vancouver we have what is known as the Alvin building, of which the minister has heard a good deal


in the last few years. It should have everything that could be imagined, in view of the price the government paid for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: Now surely we are not going to start that again.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext:
This building is the headquarters of the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service. Many people go in there each day, and frequently they must wait for hours before they receive attention from the officials. On February 9 these questions of mine appeared in Hansard:
1.	Are washroom facilities available in the Alvin building, Vancouver, British Columbia, for the use of persons waiting to interview employees of the national employment service or the unemployment insurance commission?
2.	If not, will provision be made for such facilities?
The answer to the first question was No, and to the second-
No. The Department of Public Works does not provide public washrooms in government buildings under its jurisdiction.
I can understand that in respect of most buildings that is a proper policy, but I do suggest that in a building of this type there should be washroom facilities. We had the same difficulty in connection with the immigration building at the boundary point of Douglas. The first plans did not call for any washroom facilities, but after protests had been made in the house the plans were changed and provision was made.
Different organizations in Vancouver have requested that a similar change be made in connection with the Alvin building. Can the minister tell the committee whether something can be done along this line?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: We are certainly considering the question of having washrooms in our public buildings. However, the difficulty is to know where to stop. Once we have put washrooms in one public building, are we expected to put them in the three thousand buildings we occupy across the country? The problem is greater than it would appear at first glance. I can understand that it may have been justified in connection with the immigration building. However, I am told there are not many such buildings, indeed, that the one at Douglas may be the only one. If we do it in a building dealing with unemployment insurance, why should we not do it in a post office building?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: People do not have to wait in a post office.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext:

place in which they can meet, and if washroom facilities were provided it would become a public place. It is really a complicated problem. All I can say is that the department will continue to consider it with a view to finding some solution. However, I would not be prepared to commit myself.

speechtext: I am asking only that the department consider the Alvin building.

Supply

Public Works open to him. As a matter of fact my submission is that counties such as ours, with such great needs for federal public works, should be visited occasionally by the Minister of Public Works.
The first matter I would submit to the attention of the minister is one dealing with new undertakings. I know I am treading on dangerous ground when I refer to new undertakings. However, these are new works which I submit are of vital importance to three very important fishing communities in the northwestern section of my county of Gloucester.
I would ask the minister to consider seriously the possibility of constructing landing accommodation and providing shelters for our fishermen at Miscou Lighthouse or Miscou Point where there is an almost natural harbour provided at Lake Fry. I wish also to underline the necessity of providing similar accommodation for fishermen at Island River and Little Pokemouche.
Second, I would stress the importance of major repairs to three very important public wharves, those at Shippigan, Lameque and Lower Caraquet. I hope the minister will see fit to place something in the supplementary estimates to provide these wharves with their much-needed repairs.
Finally I would stress again the importance of dredging Shippigan gully. I would state that Shippigan gully is the most important entrance for the whole fishing fleet of Gloucester county, as it is the gateway between the gulf of St. Lawrence with its great fishing banks and Shippigan harbour, and thence to the Baie de Chaleur. I am informed there has been absolutely no dredging at Shippigan gully for the last five years. With the moving sands and strong currents at that point, it is high time something was done.
These were the three matters I wished to submit to the minister. Before taking my seat I would ask him to explain why the estimates for 1953-54 show a decrease of 8445,000 for New Brunswick, but an increase of $785,000 for Nova Scotia. I know the minister has already intimated that he does not like comparisons. I do not wish to elaborate upon any such comparisons, and I am not at all jealous of what Nova Scotia has received. However, I would ask for an explanation as to why New Brunswick, with such great needs, should this year be faced with a decrease in the estimates, when at the same time there is an increase for Nova Scotia.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: I should like to ask one or two questions with respect to this item. To begin with, I should like to ask the minister what is the nature of the work to be done at Lac La Ronge. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext:
This amount is required for improvements consisting mainly of the construction of a wharf with a landing head or "L" to provide urgently needed facilities for ever-increasing water-borne traffic. La Ronge is the centre of a rapidly expanding area of various activities consisting of mining, fishing and the tourist trade. It is the northern terminus of a road from Prince Albert. It is also a base for aircraft on both wheels and pontoons. All freight for more northerly points passes through La Ronge and is transshipped by boat, cat-train or plane, all of which would use the proposed landing facilities.
The proposed work consists of the construction of a rock-filled timber cribwork wharf 66 feet by 16 feet with a landing head or "L" 59 feet by 16 feet and a rock and gravel approach 55 feet long. The estimated cost is $10,000, and the work is to be done by day labour.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext:
I am not one of those who make application for expenditures from time to time unless I believe those expenditures will be self-liquidating in their result. I think this is a very worthy piece of work on the part of the minister, and one that deserves further expansion. I believe the development that is taking place in northern Saskatchewan is unknown to the people of Canada generally, particularly in connection with uranium prospecting and development. Lac La Ronge serves that northern area and I should like to see extensive improvements made there, because the situation today is such that the available facilities are not capable of meeting the demands of uranium and other mining developments.
During recent years most of the developments in northern Saskatchewan have been advantageous not particularly to northern Saskatchewan but generally speaking to the city of Edmonton. We in northern Saskatchewan believe that, with the potential uranium area in that part of Canada, the area immediately adjacent to and north and west of Lac La Ronge, if anticipated prospects are eventually achieved that area will produce uranium to such an extent within a very few years that it will be the greatest uranium area in all the world. That is not exaggeration.
Recently when I was in New York, as were two or three of the ministers of the crown, in connection with the Town Hall meetings, I had the opportunity of meeting various New York industrialists. They realize something of the potentialities of northern Saskatchewan. When I ask for improvements which will assure a greater measure of air transportation there, I do not lose

sight of the fact that in addition to facilities for air transportation, facilities should also be made available, in the interests of the country as a whole and the common aims of the NATO countries, to achieve the largest potential possible in mineral development, particularly uranium development. I think the federal government should give consideration not only to assistance such as this, which is infinitesimal compared with the possibilities of the area, but that there should be cooperation between the Department of Public Works and the defence department in providing landing facilities in the area, and also co-operation with the province of Saskatchewan in the building of roads so that ground transportation will be available.
As it is now, the tremendous impetus that would be given to the country as a whole through uranium, gold and other mineral production will be held back unless something in the nature of a national development policy is achieved through co-operation between the dominion and provincial governments, in which policy the Department of Public Works will play its part. This item of $10,000 is more or less a token item. It will achieve all that $10,000 can achieve in providing the necessary water facilities to permit the landing of aircraft, in particular. But I do impress upon the minister, and through him the government, the need of something being done. Now that uranium is required as it has never been required before, and with a uranium potential available unequalled anywhere in the world, cooperation should be achieved between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys so that the available resources may be exploited for the benefit of our country and the achievement of our defence purposes.
I do not want to speak at length, but I wish to place this matter before the minister. I know his personal interest in achieving a national policy for Canada under which each of us recognizes the need of full development in every other part of Canada. In recent months mineral resources have been discovered and development has been taking place in all provinces of Canada except one. This area of northern Saskatchewan, with its tremendous possibilities in the world of today, with the challenge of communism having been held back in large measure by the fact that we are becoming powerful in atomic weapons, is an area that deserves full support from the government.
An item like this, welcome as it is, is but a drop in the bucket compared with the expenditure that should be made there in order to assure that available resources will
Supply-Public Works be developed. After all resources, however great, of minerals or uranium or other metals that go into the forging of the shield of freedom will be worthless should communism march, unless they have in fact been developed.
One thing that is holding back development in northern Saskatchewan is the lack of available transportation facilities on land. We have them in the air, although we have no airport facilities worthy of the name in the city of Prince Albert which is the northern outpost in our province. This vote is but the beginning, I hope, of further votes that will have to be made if the available resources, now estimated at $200 million a year in uranium production, are to be made available for our common defence.

No. If we may get out of the interior and to the coast for a few minutes I would like to say that the particular section of the coast of British Columbia which runs from the north end of Vancouver island to the Alaskan boundary is the part of British Columbia for which I am the mouthpiece down here. As the minister knows, it is a section of the country where a large number of small communities are entirely dependent on water transportation for their economic livelihood. I wish to bring one or two of them to his attention, and I propose to deal with them together to save the minister's valuable time.
Even though I know how anxious he is to see this item passed, I am going to take a minute to say on the floor of this house how much I and the other residents of the coast of British Columbia feel indebted to his officers in the New Westminster office for the thorough, complete, and very sympathetic interest and knowledge they have of the problems we have in those small communities.
In the particulars under this item on page 425 there is a reference to harbour improvements at Bella Coola. I would like to urge upon the minister the fact that Bella Coola is one of those communities entirely isolated by every other form of transportation except steamship. There is no road, there is no railway, and there is no commercial air line. This item, which to a very large extent is a revote, has been in the estimates for more than one year, and I would urge upon the minister that he show to the people of Bella Coola that kindness of heart for which he is so famed and proceed to have this small harbour job done this year. The cost is only $49,000.

I also wish to express to the minister the appreciation of the people concerned for the dredging votes for Delkatla slough at Masset on the north end of the Queen Charlotte islands and for Inverness passage near Prince Rupert, for which tenders have been called and I understand it is the department's intention to let those contracts this year.

I cannot emphasize too strongly that in both these cases dredging is required because there is now not sufficient water there to enable the large halibut packers and vessels of that type to come in, unload or lie during low tide. Therefore I hope the minister will take one further step, after providing funds, and make certain that the work is done.
That leads me to one other point I wish to make in connection with dredging. The department has decided this year to undertake two major dredging projects on the north coast. That means it will have dredging equipment in that area, either of its own or under contract. It has taken a long time to get dredging equipment in there, and if it gets away it will take a long time to bring it back, because they will not bring in dredging equipment to do a little $5,000 or $10,000 job. Therefore I urge that certain small dredging requirements be undertaken at the present time. Two I have in mind are not included in the present estimates. The amount involved would be small, and I think there would be time to include them in the supplementary estimates.
At this time I am not asking for a major expenditure. I would urge, however, the dredging of Skidegate channel, between the north and south islands of the Queen Charlotte islands group. That is the only way one can get to the mainland of British Columbia from the west coast of the Queen Charlotte islands, without going around the north or south end or, in other words, without a voyage of about 180 additional miles.
It is a big undertaking to make a real, deep channel through there; but that is not what we are asking. We are asking only for a channel which would enable ships of the size of small packers and fishing vessels to go through the channel. I am not asking even that it be dredged so they could go through at low tide, only that they may be able to go through at half tide to high tide, with reasonable safety.
This is not a little, local proposition asked for only by the residents of a small community. It has attracted the attention of the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative association, which represents all the fishermen on the north coast, and the suggestion has been heartily endorsed by them. It has also attracted the attention of the fisheries association of British Columbia.
I should like to read to the minister part of a letter written to me by that association. It is dated February 14 of this year, and says;
I have been directed by the fisheries association of British Columbia to write you in connection with Skidegate narrows and the possibility of dredging this channel. For many years this matter has been discussed in the fishing industry ge:ier-

ally, and we believe, in the department of defence, but to date nothing conclusive has developed.
When Mr. Sinclair, Minister of Fisheries, was in Vancouver we brought this request to his attention and he suggested that we communicate with you as you were very familiar with the district and would be appreciative of our problem.
The fisheries association suggests that immediate consideration be given to the dredging of Skide-gate narrows. During last year's heavy run of pinks on the west coast of the Queen Charlotte islands, there were many delays in the dispatching of the fish to the canneries on the mainland. There were delays in the movement of boats north and south on account of weather, and their inability to navigate through the channel. We believe that such a program would add materially to the protection of fishermen, the efficiency of fishing in this area, and assure the processors of receiving fish in a better condition, which is foremost in our minds.
Then there is the matter of the use of such a channel for defence purposes, crash boats, and other services required in the country's defence.
We recommend, therefore, that a survey be carried out as soon as possible as we feel that the dredging of the channel does not present too great an engineering problem, and believe that the cost of such a project would not be prohibitive.
We would like you to consider this letter as a formal request to initiate the interest of all those concerned. All fishing organizations will support us in this project.
I believe it is the opinion of some officials in the Department of Public Works that this project involves greater expense and a bigger undertaking than they would feel justified in promising at this time. I suggest to them, with all deference, that the people who are actually making their living in the fishing industry on that coast know that channel very well. They know what they want. They know they are not asking for a St. Lawrence seaway; they are asking for the removal of certain obstructions. They are asking for the clearing of brush from points on shore so that one can see from point to point. They are asking for an expenditure which I suggest with respect would be well under $50,000; and $50,000 is a pretty small sum to ask when compared with the value of the fisheries production on the Pacific coast.
Then, on the subject of dredging equipment, I would refer to Digby island, and the little community of Dodge Cove. This is a community of some 60 or less fishing families who make their homes there the year round. It is the site of a small saw mill and a reasonably good-sized privately-owned boat-building establishment. They have a harbour which has a sand bottom, and which should be dredged to a depth of approximately six to eight feet. This would not be necessary over a large area, but only sufficient to afford berthing space for ships to lie in there. These would be fishing boats, and not large ones at that. They could lie in there over low tide without their keels
Supply-Public Works
touching bottom and, with the water going out, the ships falling over on their sides.
The approach to the harbour is only a small item. May I emphasize to the minister that if we had no dredging equipment in the district perhaps I would not be justified in asking him to dredge Dodge cove, or to go to the expense of bringing in dredging equipment from the south to do that work. However, with dredging equipment in the area, as there will be this year, it is in the interests of economy and of the residents of the area, as well as the interests of the fishing industry as a whole, that these small dredging jobs be done now, while they can be done cheaply and quickly.

I understand that this is really an important question. The hon. member knows how this board was set up by agreement with British Columbia. I have quite a long expose of the whole situation, and I have a list of the members representing the federal government and the provincial government. I received, I think about a year ago, an interim report from this board, and I am told that I have received no other report. I think I did show that report or give a resume of it to the members, but it was in such general terms that we could not base any immediate works upon it. This is a survey and study of the whole Fraser river basin. The people on that board seem to have quite a reputation. They are outstanding citizens and engineers.
This is the information I have been given. This amount of $137,500 is required to pay the federal government's share of the cost of investigations proposed, to be carried out during 1953-54 by the dominion-provincial board, Fraser river basin. The board was established by authority of order in council P.C. 247/288 dated January 22, 1949, for the purpose of conducting an investigation to determine the improvements which might be undertaken to develop the water resources of the Fraser

Supply-Public Works valley, British Columbia, in the interest of fish and wildlife, water power, flood control, irrigation, reclamation of wet lands and other beneficial purposes. It is for that reason that there are representatives of these different departments on that board. The board consists of officials of the provincial government of British Columbia and the government of Canada. The province of British Columbia and the government of Canada will share the cost of the said survey and report equally.
The amount asked for during 1953-54 is $137,500. This amount is to cover the federal government's share, 50 per cent, of the cost of the following work proposed to be carried on in 1953-54: Aerial photography and bathymetric survey, $75,000; Department of Resources and Development, gauging stations and metering, $13,200; Department of Fisheries, Canada, gauging stations, $4,250; department of lands and forests, water rights branch, flood control, power and sedimentation investigation, $74,500. The board will spend $34,000 for damsite exploration; $22,500 for pollution investigation; $3,500 for land use mapping; $31,500 for administration, salaries and operation. The total amount is $258,450. The federal government's share is $129,225. The amount necessary for the department to meet monthly payments pending receipt of the province's share of the cost is $8,275. To the best of my ability I have given an outline of the way this money is to be spent, giving the details of the work that is to be done and the amount stated.
As to the progress they are making, as the hon. member says it is a long-winded investigation and I suppose when they have all their data gathered together they will make a final and comprehensive report which will be the basis of the works that may be undertaken by the federal government in conjunction with the provincial government. I realize that it is most important to that province that we continue these surveys and research.

I am going to resist the temptation, Mr. Chairman, I assure you and the minister, to make any sort of a speech on this project, although I can assure the minister it is probably one the importance of which is not readily apparent to him or to the members of the house. This Fraser river system takes in the larger part of the dry belt area of the province. It may be' news to the minister, but I want to impress upon him that the Fraser river system takes in far more than what is known as the constituency of Fraser Valley. Its tributaries flow through my own riding, and the problems of irrigation, power development and flood control are of immense importance to us there.

I am sure the minister remembers the number of times I have seen him in his office or have come over to sit beside him in the house to discuss this matter and express the view that, although we appreciate the painstaking and methodical care that must be shown in developing a program to deal with this problem, it does concern us that there is not more positive progress evident. With the greatest respect, I think it is fair to suggest to the minister that the outline he has given us tonight is really nothing more than an outline of expenditures to cover further studies. It does not do very much to reassure us that there is that sense of urgency in developing this work which we sought to impress upon him and have him in turn, as the responsible minister in this government, impart to and impress upon his officials on that board who are undertaking this work.
I do not want to labour any particular point. We understand that this may be the last opportunity we will have to discuss this matter with the minister because other activities may absorb his attention. May I suggest to him that if he does nothing else but get this work going, and get some positive results, he will have erected for himself a lasting monument to his career as Minister of Public Works. Not in jest but with the greatest good will in the world and appreciation of the minister's interest in the whole of Canada, which embraces of course the interests of the province of British Columbia, I do ask him to give this more than just a passing interest. I ask him to devote some time and some effort, if I may use that word, toward impressing upon all the officials in charge of this work the importance of producing a concrete plan and program of development upon which some initial steps may be taken before the close of this fiscal year which we are discussing now. If he does that, and if he takes even one positive step toward construction, the minister may be satisfied that his name will go down in the annals of British Columbia as one of its greatest benefactors.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. gentlemen for the co-operation and good will and help they have given me. I was thinking during these three days that if hon. gentlemen had had, as I had, requests from all of these gentlemen in the House of Commons they would be astounded at the amount I am asking parliament to vote-as compared to the total of the requests of all of the gentlemen.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Eglinton wish to say something more on this item?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: I have indicated my desire to be co-operative with the minister, and I do not wish to delay the conclusion of the estimates of his department. At the same time I hope the minister will give the information to the house. It is not just for myself, it is a matter of interest to others.

information tomorrow at the opening, and I
Supply-Public Works will just table it or give it to the hon. gentleman. I think I will have time to get the information tomorrow morning, and I give the assurance that tomorrow, or Monday at the latest, I will give the information to the house.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: I thank the minister; but has he looked into this matter carefully himself? After all, it is a very substantial amount to be spent on the furnishing of the prime minister's residence, which was furnished just two years ago.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: Here we are this year with another expenditure of $4,000. We have not the information here, so I am left with the alternative of asking the minister if he has looked into the matter personally and is satisfied that this is something that is required. It is a very substantial amount after the fabulous sums spent on this residence and its furnishings two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext:
If I was not satisfied that it was required I would have refused to bring it before the treasury board and before the cabinet; but there is no home in this country that I know of that does not require something to be done in it every year. I happen to own a home and I would like to skip a year in which I would not have to make certain expenditures.
Whilst I am Minister of Public Works I will not allow this residence to get into a state of disrepair. I am going to try to keep it in good repair, but the hon. gentleman will get any information he wants. He has that assurance from me.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: We are not discussing repairs at the moment. This item covers furnishings; and there are not very many homes that spend $4,000 a year on furnishings, especially after being set up handsomely just two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF MACNAB REPORT
speechtext: This is included in an estimated expenditure of $10,500 which was passed yesterday. I promised that I would give the details of that vote, and I will.
